title: Gut Hormone Tumours: VIPoma, Gastrinoma and Urine 5-HIAA
summary: Learn how VIPoma (WDHA), gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) and carcinoid syndrome are proven in the laboratory: secretory-diarrhoea features and VIP sampling, fasting gastrin read with gastric pH and the secretin test, and a properly prepared 24-hour urine 5-HIAA.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 23 Hit 8 (WDHA/VIPoma), Hit 9 (24-hour urinary 5-HIAA for carcinoid syndrome) and Hit 11 (gastrinoma/Zollinger-Ellison). Checked against Una Cidon 2022, Magi 2023, Franchina 2024, Rossi 2021, Arasaradnam 2018 (BSG), Kerolles 2025 (all Europe PMC full text) and Ito 2012 (read by the lesson author via a page-fetch tool, last ~25,000 characters not read; at the independent fact-check the PMC page was blocked by a browser-verification check and only its abstract was re-read, so no taught statement relies on Ito 2012 alone). Qualified: the secretin criterion in the sources read is a gastrin rise of at least 120 pg/mL, not >200 ng/L within 15 min, and the diagnostic pair is gastrin >10× ULN with pH <2 (register flag rv-secretin-gastrin-criteria); the reviewer’s “>90% sensitive and specific” for urine 5-HIAA is not reproduced (BSG 88%; Kerolles cites 77%/97%) (register flag rv-5hiaa-accuracy); “octreotide controls symptoms in >90%” was not confirmed (one cohort in Azizian 2022: 66.7% significant antisecretory activity with somatostatin analogues alone) (register flag rv-vipoma-octreotide-response). Not taught: stool volumes up to 30 L/day, the fasting gastrin >150 ng/L with pH <3 “suggestive” rule and basal acid output >15 mmol/h (the BAO figure appears in Ito 2012 as a separate criterion), octreotide response rate. The NCBI Bookshelf VIPoma page was blocked by a captcha and was not read.

objectives: Recognise the WDHA picture of VIPoma and the laboratory features of secretory diarrhoea, and state how a VIP sample should be collected.
Interpret fasting gastrin with gastric pH and the secretin test, and name the common causes of hypergastrinaemia.
Describe patient preparation and limits of the 24-hour urine 5-HIAA for carcinoid syndrome.

scenes.title: Three loud tumours
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three patients. (1) Watery diarrhoea of about 4 L a day that continues while the patient is fasting, with serum potassium 2.6 mmol/L. (2) Recurrent duodenal ulcers and diarrhoea in a patient taking a proton-pump inhibitor (PPI); fasting gastrin is raised. (3) Flushing and diarrhoea with liver lesions; a 24-hour urine for 5-HIAA is collected the day after a meal of bananas, tomatoes and walnuts. Question token: “Which hormone, and is the test valid?”

cues.text: Invented case one: about four litres of watery diarrhoea a day, still running while the patient is fasting, with a very low potassium.
Case two: recurrent duodenal ulcers and diarrhoea, in a patient on a proton-pump inhibitor, with a raised fasting gastrin.
Case three: flushing, diarrhoea and liver lesions, and a urine 5-HIAA collected after bananas, tomatoes and walnuts. Which hormone, and is each test valid?

props.label: Which hormone, and is the test valid?

scenes.title: Three hormones, three jobs
scenes.altText: Schematic: three hormone cards. VIP (vasoactive intestinal peptide): raises cAMP in intestinal cells, driving water and electrolyte secretion into the bowel lumen, and inhibits gastric acid secretion. Gastrin: made by gastric G cells, stimulates gastric acid secretion. Serotonin: made from tryptophan; in the gut mainly by enterochromaffin cells, mostly in the small bowel; its urinary metabolite is 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA). Bottom token: each functioning neuroendocrine tumour is proven by the hormone (or metabolite) it overproduces.

cues.text: Gut neuroendocrine tumours are recognised by the hormone they overproduce. Three are classic exam material.
Vasoactive intestinal peptide, VIP, raises cyclic AMP in intestinal cells. Water and electrolytes pour into the bowel, and gastric acid secretion is inhibited.
Gastrin, from the G cells of the stomach, drives gastric acid secretion.
Serotonin is made from tryptophan; in the gut, mainly by enterochromaffin cells, mostly in the small bowel. Its urinary breakdown product is 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, 5-HIAA.

props.label: Functioning tumour → proven by its hormone

scenes.title: VIPoma and carcinoid syndrome: what proves them
scenes.altText: Left card, VIPoma (WDHA: watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, achlorhydria): stool volume below 700 mL/day virtually rules it out; volumes usually exceed 3 L/day; the diarrhoea persists through a 72-hour fast (secretory, unlike osmotic diarrhoea); stool osmolality is accounted for by electrolytes, osmotic gap below 50; serum VIP is raised. Sample token: draw VIP while the patient has diarrhoea (release fluctuates), add a protease inhibitor, keep frozen, and repeat to confirm. Right card, carcinoid syndrome: 24-hour urine 5-HIAA is the recommended biochemical test; a tryptophan- and serotonin-free diet for 48 to 72 hours before collection (foods such as bananas, tomatoes, plums, pineapple, avocado, eggplant, walnuts); some drugs interfere; collection is often repeated on two consecutive days because of day-to-day variation. Serum 5-HIAA is an emerging alternative.

cues.text: VIPoma causes the WDHA picture: watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, achlorhydria. Stool volume below about seven hundred millilitres a day virtually rules it out; most patients pass more than three litres.
It is a secretory diarrhoea: it carries on through a seventy-two-hour fast, and stool electrolytes explain the stool osmolality, so the osmotic gap is below fifty. A raised serum VIP proves it.
VIP release fluctuates, so draw the sample during diarrhoea, add a protease inhibitor, keep it frozen, and repeat it to confirm the diagnosis.

For carcinoid syndrome, the recommended test is a twenty-four-hour urine 5-HIAA, after forty-eight to seventy-two hours free of tryptophan- and serotonin-rich foods such as bananas, tomatoes and walnuts. Some drugs interfere too.
Because output varies from day to day, two consecutive collections are often advised. Serum 5-HIAA is an emerging alternative.

props.label: VIP: draw in diarrhoea · inhibitor · frozen

scenes.title: Proving a gastrinoma
scenes.altText: Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) workup as schematic cards. Card 1: diagnosis needs inappropriate hypergastrinaemia PLUS high acid: fasting serum gastrin (FSG) more than 10 times the upper limit (usually above 1000 pg/mL, which equals ng/L) with gastric pH below 2 establishes it. Card 2: FSG raised less than 10-fold with pH below 2 (about 60% of patients): exclude other causes, then secretin test — 2 U/kg IV bolus, gastrin sampled before and up to 30 minutes after; a rise of at least 120 pg/mL at any sample is positive. Token: chronic PPI use raises gastrin and masks the syndrome; atrophic gastritis gives high gastrin with LOW acid. About 25% of gastrinomas occur with MEN1. Hook answers card.

cues.text: Gastrin is only meaningful next to stomach acid. A fasting gastrin more than ten times the upper limit, usually above one thousand picograms per millilitre, with a gastric pH below two, establishes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

About sixty percent have a pH below two but a smaller gastrin rise. Exclude other causes, then give secretin, two units per kilogram intravenously. A gastrin rise of at least one hundred and twenty picograms per millilitre is positive.
The common mimics: chronic proton-pump inhibitor use raises gastrin, and atrophic gastritis raises gastrin because acid is low. About a quarter of gastrinomas occur with MEN1.

Back to the hook. Case one: measure VIP during diarrhoea. Case two: the PPI clouds both gastrin and pH; specialist workup with pH and secretin testing. Case three: repeat the 5-HIAA after a serotonin-free diet.

props.title: Hook answers
lines: 2 PPI clouds gastrin + pH → specialist workup

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “High gastrin = gastrinoma” (✓ gastrin must be judged with gastric pH; PPIs and atrophic gastritis raise gastrin with low acid); “Secretin test is positive only above a 200 rise” (✓ the criterion in the reviews read is a rise of at least 120 pg/mL); “A 5-HIAA after bananas and walnuts is valid” (✓ tryptophan/serotonin-rich foods can cause false positives; collect after a 48–72 h restricted diet).

cues.text: Trap one: a high gastrin means gastrinoma. No: gastrin must be read with gastric pH. Proton-pump inhibitors and atrophic gastritis raise gastrin while acid is low.
Trap two: the secretin test is positive only with a rise over two hundred. The criterion in current reviews is a rise of at least one hundred and twenty picograms per millilitre.
Trap three: a urine 5-HIAA after bananas and walnuts is valid. No: those foods can give false positives. Collect after a restricted diet.

props.title: ✗ “High gastrin = gastrinoma.”
lines: ✓ Read with pH; PPI + atrophic gastritis mimic

scenes.title: Flood, burn, flush
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “VIP FLOODS the bowel (and turns the acid tap off); gastrin BURNS with acid (so check the pH); serotonin FLUSHES the face and leaves 5-HIAA in the urine.” Tokens: flood = VIP · burn = gastrin + pH · flush = 5-HIAA. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: VIP floods the bowel and turns the acid tap off. Gastrin burns with acid, so always check the pH. Serotonin flushes the face and leaves 5-HIAA in the urine.

Where it breaks: diarrhoea is common in gastrinoma too, and it settles with acid suppression; carcinoid syndrome usually means liver metastases, not just a primary tumour; and hormone reference intervals depend on the assay.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “VIPoma: > 3 L secretory diarrhoea, fasting-persistent, VIP drawn in symptoms”, “Gastrin > 10× + pH < 2 or secretin rise ≥ 120 · urine 5-HIAA after diet”.

cues.text: Prove each gut hormone tumour with the right sample: VIPoma by large-volume secretory diarrhoea and a VIP drawn during symptoms, gastrinoma by fasting gastrin read with a gastric pH below 2 or a secretin rise of at least 120 pg/mL, and carcinoid syndrome by a 24-hour urine 5-HIAA collected after a serotonin-free diet.

props.label: VIPoma: > 3 L secretory, fasting-persistent · VIP in symptoms
Gastrin > 10× + pH < 2 or secretin ≥ 120 · 5-HIAA after diet

explanation.what: Plain language: some gut tumours flood the body with one hormone, and each is caught by measuring that hormone (or its breakdown product) in the right patient, at the right time, after the right preparation. Scientific terms: vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), VIPoma, WDHA (Verner-Morrison) syndrome, secretory diarrhoea, stool osmotic gap; gastrin, gastrinoma, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES), fasting serum gastrin (FSG), secretin stimulation test, MEN1; serotonin, 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), carcinoid syndrome.
explanation.why: VIP drives intestinal secretion through cAMP and suppresses gastric acid, so stool volume stays huge even when the patient fasts and potassium is lost. Gastrin drives acid, so true gastrinoma combines high gastrin with high acid, whereas PPIs and atrophic gastritis raise gastrin because acid is low. Serotonin is metabolised to 5-HIAA, so dietary serotonin and tryptophan can raise urine 5-HIAA without a tumour.
explanation.measure: VIPoma: stool <700 mL/day virtually excludes it, usually >3 L/day, persists through a 72-hour fast, osmotic gap <50; serum VIP raised (BSG gives normal <170 pg/mL and mean 675–965 pg/mL in functioning tumours; intervals are assay-specific); draw during diarrhoea, add protease inhibitor, freeze, repeat to confirm. ZES: FSG >10× ULN (usually >1000 pg/mL) with gastric pH <2 is diagnostic; otherwise secretin 2 U/kg IV with gastrin rise ≥120 pg/mL positive; about 25% of gastrinomas occur with MEN1. Carcinoid syndrome: 24-hour urine 5-HIAA after a 48–72 h tryptophan/serotonin-free diet, often on two consecutive days; serum 5-HIAA emerging.
explanation.differs: Secretory (VIPoma: persists when fasting, small osmotic gap) vs osmotic diarrhoea (stops with fasting); gastrinoma (high gastrin + pH <2) vs PPI use or atrophic gastritis (high gastrin, low acid); urine 5-HIAA vs serum serotonin (not recommended, low specificity).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the tumour from WDHA, choose the next step for a moderately raised gastrin with pH <2 (secretin test), recognise PPIs and atrophic gastritis as gastrin mimics, or spot a 5-HIAA collected without dietary preparation.

mnemonic.text: VIP FLOODS the bowel (and turns the acid tap off); gastrin BURNS with acid (so check the pH); serotonin FLUSHES the face and leaves 5-HIAA in the urine.
mnemonic.explanation: Links each tumour to its hormone, its main effect and its laboratory proof.
mnemonic.limitation: Diarrhoea is also common in gastrinoma; carcinoid syndrome usually reflects liver metastases; hormone reference intervals and cut-offs are assay-specific.

analogyLimitations: Accuracy figures come from individual studies and reviews; assays and cut-offs differ.
takeaway: Prove each gut hormone tumour with the right sample: VIPoma by large-volume secretory diarrhoea and a VIP drawn during symptoms, gastrinoma by fasting gastrin read with a gastric pH below 2 or a secretin rise of at least 120 pg/mL, and carcinoid syndrome by a 24-hour urine 5-HIAA collected after a serotonin-free diet.

questions.stem: A patient off acid-suppressing drugs has recurrent duodenal ulcers, a fasting serum gastrin of 600 pg/mL (upper limit 100 pg/mL) and a gastric pH of 1.5. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.rationale: Correct. With pH below 2 but gastrin less than 10 times the upper limit, other causes are excluded and the secretin test is used; a rise of at least 120 pg/mL is positive.
Incorrect. Gastrin is only 6 times the upper limit; the diagnostic pair is more than 10-fold elevation with pH below 2.
Incorrect. Atrophic gastritis raises gastrin because acid is low; a pH of 1.5 shows high acid.

options.text: Start a PPI and repeat the gastrin in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Incorrect. PPIs themselves raise gastrin and mask the syndrome, making the repeat uninterpretable.

questions.stem: Which finding best supports a VIPoma in a patient with chronic watery diarrhoea and hypokalaemia?

options.text: Stool volume of about 4 L/day that continues through a 72-hour fast, with a stool osmotic gap below 50
options.rationale: Correct. VIPoma causes large-volume secretory diarrhoea that persists with fasting and is explained by stool electrolytes.

options.text: Diarrhoea that stops when the patient fasts
options.rationale: Incorrect. Resolution with fasting points to an osmotic diarrhoea.
Incorrect. Stool volumes below about 700 mL/day virtually rule out a VIPoma.
Incorrect. VIP inhibits gastric acid; hypo- or achlorhydria is typical. High acid suggests gastrinoma.

questions.stem: A 24-hour urine 5-HIAA is mildly raised in a patient who ate bananas, tomatoes and walnuts the day before and during collection. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Possibly a false positive; repeat after 48–72 hours of a tryptophan- and serotonin-free diet
options.rationale: Correct. Serotonin- and tryptophan-rich foods can raise urine 5-HIAA without a tumour.
Incorrect. Dietary intake can explain a raised result; preparation was inadequate.

options.text: The diet causes false negatives, so the true value is higher
options.rationale: Incorrect. These foods cause false positives, not false negatives.

options.text: Replace it with a serum serotonin level
options.rationale: Incorrect. Circulating serotonin is not recommended because of low specificity; serum 5-HIAA, not serotonin, is the emerging alternative.

claims.text: VIP raises cAMP-driven intestinal secretion and inhibits acid; gastrin from G cells drives acid; serotonin from enterochromaffin cells, metabolised to urinary 5-HIAA.
WDHA; stool <700 mL/day virtually excludes, usually >3 L/day; persists through 72-h fast; osmotic gap <50; VIP raised; sample during diarrhoea with protease inhibitor, frozen, repeated.

FSG >10× ULN (usually >1000 pg/mL) with pH <2 diagnostic; ~60% need further testing; secretin 2 U/kg IV, rise ≥120 pg/mL positive; chronic PPI use and atrophic gastritis raise gastrin with low acid; about 25% of gastrinomas with MEN1.
24-hour urine 5-HIAA recommended; 48–72 h tryptophan/serotonin-free diet; drug interference; two collections; serum 5-HIAA emerging; serum serotonin not recommended.
Reviewer details not taught: octreotide controls VIPoma symptoms in >90%; stool up to 30 L/day; gastrin >150 ng/L with pH <3 suggestive; >90% sensitivity and specificity of urine 5-HIAA.
claims.note: Not confirmed in the sources read; see register flags rv-5hiaa-accuracy and rv-vipoma-octreotide-response.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 23 Hit 11 gives a positive secretin test as a gastrin rise >200 ng/L within 15 min and the diagnostic pair as gastrin >1000 ng/L with basal acid output >15 mmol/h. Franchina 2024 uses a rise of ≥120 pg/mL (= ng/L) at any sample up to 30 min after 2 U/kg IV secretin, and Magi 2023 and Rossi 2021 give gastrin >10× ULN (usually >1000) with gastric pH <2 as diagnostic; the lesson teaches the source criteria (register flag rv-secretin-gastrin-criteria).

Ch. 23 Hit 9 says urinary 5-HIAA is >90% sensitive and >90% specific. Arasaradnam 2018 (BSG) gives 88%, Kerolles 2025 cites sensitivity 77% and specificity 97%, and Franchina 2024 reports low sensitivity across NETs; the lesson teaches 5-HIAA as the recommended test without the >90% figure (register flag rv-5hiaa-accuracy).

Ch. 23 Hit 8 says octreotide controls VIPoma symptoms in >90%. Una Cidon 2022 describes somatostatin analogues as reducing VIP secretion, with diarrhoea control reported in more than 50% of patients and significant improvement in 25%, and one cohort cited by Azizian 2022 reported significant antisecretory activity in 66.7% on somatostatin analogues alone; the figure is not taught (register flag rv-vipoma-octreotide-response).
